claim: SLAMF6 is a homotypic receptor of the Ig-superfamily.
source: SLAMF6 is a homotypic receptor of the Ig-superfamily whose exact role in immune modulation has remained elusive.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of SLAMF6.

claim: SLAMF6 is constitutively expressed on resting and activated T cells.
source: Its constitutive expression on resting and activated T cells precludes it from being a bona fide exhaustion marker.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1.

claim: Activated Pmel-1xSLAMF6 -/- CD8+ T cells displayed improved polyfunctionality and strong tumor cytolysis.
source: Activated Pmel-1xSLAMF6 -/- CD8+ T cells displayed improved polyfunctionality and strong tumor cytolysis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: T-bet was the dominant transcription factor in Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- cells.
source: T-bet was the dominant transcription factor in Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- cells, and upon activation, they acquired an effector-memory phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 6D.

claim: Upon activation, Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- cells acquired an effector-memory phenotype.
source: T-bet was the dominant transcription factor in Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- cells, and upon activation, they acquired an effector-memory phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3G-H.

claim: Adoptive transfer of Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- T cells to melanoma-bearing mice resulted in lasting tumor regression.
source: Adoptive transfer of Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- T cells to melanoma-bearing mice resulted in lasting tumor regression in contrast to temporary responses achieved with Pmel-1 T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by in vivo tumor growth data in Figure 4H-J.

claim: Adoptive transfer of Pmel-1 T cells to melanoma-bearing mice resulted in temporary responses.
source: Adoptive transfer of Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- T cells to melanoma-bearing mice resulted in lasting tumor regression in contrast to temporary responses achieved with Pmel-1 T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by in vivo tumor growth data in Figure 4H-J.

claim: LAG-3 expression was elevated in the SLAMF6 -/- cells.
source: LAG-3 expression was elevated in the SLAMF6 -/- cells, and the addition of the LAG-3-blocking antibody to the adoptive transfer protocol improved the SLAMF6 -/- T cells and expedited the antitumor response even further.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6E.

claim: The addition of the LAG-3-blocking antibody to the adoptive transfer protocol improved the SLAMF6 -/- T cells and expedited the antitumor response.
source: LAG-3 expression was elevated in the SLAMF6 -/- cells, and the addition of the LAG-3-blocking antibody to the adoptive transfer protocol improved the SLAMF6 -/- T cells and expedited the antitumor response even further.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by in vivo data in Figure 6G-I.

claim: SLAMF6 is an inhibitory immune receptor whose absence enables powerful CD8+ T cells to eradicate tumors.
source: The results from this study support the notion that SLAMF6 is an inhibitory immune receptor whose absence enables powerful CD8+ T cells to eradicate tumors.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: The SLAM family of receptors (SFRs) is a set of six receptors expressed on hematopoietic cells.
source: The SLAM family of receptors (SFRs) is a set of six receptors expressed on hematopoietic cells (Wu and Veillette, 2016; Cannons et al., 2011; Veillette, 2010; Calpe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: All SFRs, except 2B4, are homotypic binders.
source: All SFRs, except 2B4, are homotypic binders, that is they engage the same ectodomain sequence, either in cis (same cell) or in trans (adjacent cell) configuration.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about SFRs.

claim: Most hematopoietic cell types express 3–5 members of the SLAM family.
source: Most hematopoietic cell types express 3–5 members of the SLAM family.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as general knowledge about SLAM family expression.

claim: SFRs generate signals via a bi-phasic mechanism of recruitment to tyrosines in the immunoreceptor tyrosine-based switch motifs (ITSMs) in their cytoplasmic domain.
source: SFRs generate signals via a bi-phasic mechanism of recruitment to tyrosines in the immunoreceptor tyrosine-based switch motifs (ITSMs) in their cytoplasmic domain.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about SFR signaling.

claim: SLAM associated protein (SAP) is the default adaptor of the SFRs.
source: SLAM associated protein (SAP), a small protein containing the Src homology 2 (SH2)-domain, was shown to be the default adaptor of the SFRs, interchanging with protein tyrosine phosphatases, mainly SHP-1, but also SHP-2, inositol phosphatase SHIP-1 and protein tyrosine kinase Csk (Wu and Veillette, 2016; Cannons et al., 2011; Veillette, 2010; Calpe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: SLAMF6 is also known as CD352, LY108, or NTB-A.
source: SLAMF6, also known as CD352, LY108, or NTB-A, is a homotypic SFR expressed on T cells, NK cells, B cells, and dendritic cells (Bottino et al., 2001; Zhong and Veillette, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: SLAMF6 is expressed on T cells, NK cells, B cells, and dendritic cells.
source: SLAMF6, also known as CD352, LY108, or NTB-A, is a homotypic SFR expressed on T cells, NK cells, B cells, and dendritic cells (Bottino et al., 2001; Zhong and Veillette, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Kageyama et al. linked SLAMF6 to the anchoring of T cells to their target cells, and subsequent cytolysis of the target.
source: Kageyama et al. linked SLAMF6 to the anchoring of T cells to their target cells, and subsequent cytolysis of the target (Kageyama et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Functional SAP is critical for SLAMF6 activity according to Kageyama et al.
source: According to these authors, functional SAP is critical for SLAMF6 activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction referencing Kageyama et al.'s work.

claim: In mice lacking SAP, SLAMF6 was shown to inhibit T cell function.
source: In mice lacking SAP, SLAMF6 was shown to inhibit T cell function (Kageyama et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2012; Bottino et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: There are indications that SLAMF6 plays an activating role in double-positive thymocytes.
source: There are indications that SLAMF6 plays an activating role in double-positive thymocytes (Dutta et al., 2013) along with evidence that it plays an inhibitory role in iNKT cells and CD8+ T cells (Lu et al., 2019; Eisenberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: There is evidence that SLAMF6 plays an inhibitory role in iNKT cells and CD8+ T cells.
source: There are indications that SLAMF6 plays an activating role in double-positive thymocytes (Dutta et al., 2013) along with evidence that it plays an inhibitory role in iNKT cells and CD8+ T cells (Lu et al., 2019; Eisenberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Gene expression profiles of T cell subsets link SLAMF6 to the progenitor-exhausted state.
source: Gene expression profiles of T cell subsets link SLAMF6 to the progenitor-exhausted state (Miller et al., 2019) and to the tuning of the critical number of T cells required for proper differentiation (Polonsky et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: SLAMF6 is linked to the tuning of the critical number of T cells required for proper differentiation.
source: Gene expression profiles of T cell subsets link SLAMF6 to the progenitor-exhausted state (Miller et al., 2019) and to the tuning of the critical number of T cells required for proper differentiation (Polonsky et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: After 1 day of activation, there was an initial decrease in the SLAMF6 transcript that switched to over-expression in human TILs.
source: After 1 day of activation, there was an initial decrease in the SLAMF6 transcript that switched to over-expression (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: From 3 days after activation onward, SLAMF6 receptor expression consistently increased in human TILs.
source: From 3 days after activation onward, SLAMF6 receptor expression consistently increased (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The increased SLAMF6 expression was most pronounced in T cells activated in the absence of IL-2.
source: Interestingly, the increased expression was most pronounced in T cells activated in the absence of IL-2 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1D.

claim: A similar pattern of SLAMF6 expression was observed for murine SLAMF6 receptor on Pmel-1 CD8+ T cells.
source: A similar pattern was observed for the expression of the murine SLAMF6 receptor on Pmel-1 CD8+ T cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1E.

claim: The SLAMF6 transcript appears in cluster C, rising at 6 hr of activation and staying high after that.
source: The SLAMF6 transcript appears in cluster C, rising at 6 hr of activation and staying high after that (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: Other genes in cluster C include CD44, CD28, and ICOS.
source: Other genes in cluster C are CD44, encoding a glycoprotein that takes part in T cell activation (Huet et al., 1989), and CD28 and ICOS, which encode co-stimulatory immune receptors (Turka et al., 1990; Dong et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations for the functions of these genes.

claim: SLAMF6-expressing melanoma cells co-cultured with Pmel-1 CD8+ T cells led to decreased IFN-γ secretion by the lymphocytes compared to wild-type cell line.
source: Compared to the wild-type cell line, the SLAMF6-expressing melanoma cells co-cultured with Pmel-1 CD8+ T cells led to decreased IFN-γ secretion by the lymphocytes (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA and flow cytometry data in Figure 2B and C.

claim: B16-F10/mhgp100/SLAMF6+ tumors grew more aggressively than non-modified tumors in an adoptive T cell transfer regimen.
source: The B16-F10/mhgp100/SLAMF6+ tumors grew more aggressively: on day 23, the mean tumor volume was 431 mm3 in the SLAMF6-expressing melanomas, compared to 137 mm3 in the non-modified tumors (p=0.04, Student's t-test) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by in vivo tumor growth data in Figure 2E.

claim: Trans-activation of SLAMF6 on lymphocytes inhibits the melanoma-specific CD8+ T cell response and allows rapid tumor growth.
source: These experiments show that trans-activation of SLAMF6 on lymphocytes, which in this system was achieved with the SLAMF6-expressing melanoma, inhibits the melanoma-specific CD8+ T cell response and allows rapid tumor growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the experiments with SLAMF6-expressing melanoma.

claim: Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- mouse spleens had a lower percentage (15%) of CD8+ cells compared to Pmel-1 splenocytes (24%).
source: Evaluation of the lymphocyte subsets in these mice showed a lower percentage (15%) of CD8+ cells in Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- mouse spleens compared to Pmel-1 splenocytes (24%) (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3B.

claim: The ratio of CD8+ subpopulations (naive, effector, effector memory, and central memory) was similar in both Pmel-1 and Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- mouse strains.
source: Despite the smaller percent of CD8+ cells in the spleens of the SLAMF6-deficient mice, the ratio of CD8+ subpopulations (naive, effector, effector memory, and central memory) was similar in both mouse strains (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3C.

claim: The proliferative response to peptide stimulation was preserved in Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- T cells.
source: Their proliferative response to peptide stimulation was preserved, which was mandatory to produce ample numbers of CD8+ lymphocytes for the adoptive T cell transfer regimen (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3D.

claim: CFSE dilution curves were identical in Pmel-1 and Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- mouse strains.
source: CFSE dilution curves were identical in the two mouse strains, as were the activation-induced cell death (AICD) rates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Activation-induced cell death (AICD) rates were identical in Pmel-1 and Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- mouse strains.
source: CFSE dilution curves were identical in the two mouse strains, as were the activation-induced cell death (AICD) rates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: After 3 days of activation, Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- mice had higher expression levels of CD25 and CD137 (4-1BB) activation markers.
source: After 3 days of activation, the -/- mice had higher expression levels of CD25 and CD137 (4-1BB) activation markers (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3E.

claim: Higher PD-1 expression was detected on day 7 in Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- cells.
source: In parallel, higher PD-1 expression was detected on day 7 (Figure 3F), which in this experimental context was initially taken as an indicator of activation, but was later attributed to SAP deficiency in the SLAMF6 -/- lymphocytes (see below in Results and Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3F.

claim: The expression of other SLAM family members and ligands (CD48, LY9, CD244, CD8+4, CD319) on T cells during activation was similar in Pmel-1 and Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- cells.
source: The expression of other SLAM family members and ligands (CD48, LY9, CD244, CD8+4, CD319) on T cells during activation was similar in Pmel-1 and Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Only a negligible number of the activated Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- cells remained in the naïve CD62Lhigh/CD44low state compared to 10% of the Pmel-1 cells.
source: While initially, all Pmel-1 T cells were naive, only a negligible number of the activated Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- cells remained in the naïve CD62Lhigh/CD44low state compared to 10% of the Pmel-1 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3G and H.

claim: The complete shift of the activated Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- lymphocytes towards effector and effector memory phenotypes indicates the strength of their response to activation.
source: The complete shift of the activated Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- lymphocytes towards effector and effector memory phenotypes indicates the strength of their response to activation (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3G and H.

claim: Cytokine production by Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- lymphocytes was significantly higher at all effector-to-target ratios compared to Pmel-1 lymphocytes.
source: Comparing IFN-γ secretion in response to melanoma cells by Pmel-1 versus Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- lymphocytes showed that cytokine production by the Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- lymphocytes was significantly higher at all effector-to-target ratios (p=0.05, Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA data in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- T cells produced higher levels of GM-CSF compared to Pmel-1 T cells.
source: In addition to IFN-γ, higher secretion of GM-CSF and lower levels of IL-10 and IL-13 were measured in the SLAMF6 -/- T cells (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA data in Figure 4C.

claim: Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- T cells produced lower levels of IL-10 and IL-13 compared to Pmel-1 T cells.
source: In addition to IFN-γ, higher secretion of GM-CSF and lower levels of IL-10 and IL-13 were measured in the SLAMF6 -/- T cells (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by cytokine array data in Figure 4D.

claim: Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- T cells produced higher levels of granzyme B in response to melanoma compared to Pmel-1 T cells.
source: Importantly, Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- T cells produced higher levels of granzyme B in response to melanoma compared to Pmel-1 T cells, which are already strong killers due to their TCR design (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4E and F.

claim: In the first 4 weeks post-transfer, tumor growth was inhibited in both Pmel-1 and Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- ACT groups.
source: The spider curves comparing melanoma growth following Pmel-1 versus Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- T cell transfer revealed that in the first 4 weeks post-transfer, tumor growth was inhibited in both groups.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by tumor growth data in Figure 4H.

claim: On week 4, tumors treated with Pmel-1 ACT escaped control and grew again in six of the seven animals.
source: However, on week 4, tumors treated with Pmel-1 ACT escaped control and grew again in six of the seven animals, whereas mice receiving Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- ACT survived longer, and three of the seven treated mice remained tumor-free for over 80 days (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by tumor growth data in Figure 4H.

claim: Mice receiving Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- ACT survived longer, and three of the seven treated mice remained tumor-free for over 80 days.
source: However, on week 4, tumors treated with Pmel-1 ACT escaped control and grew again in six of the seven animals, whereas mice receiving Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- ACT survived longer, and three of the seven treated mice remained tumor-free for over 80 days (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by tumor growth data in Figure 4H.

claim: Vitiligo was noted in all mice attaining complete response, showing up earlier in the SLAMF6 -/- group at the 6th week.
source: Vitiligo was noted in all mice attaining complete response, showing up earlier in the -/- group, at the 6th week, indicating the strength of the response (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by photographs in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A higher proportion of gp10025-33 tetramer+ cells was found in the draining lymph nodes of mice that had received Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- cells compared to those who had received Pmel-1 cells.
source: A higher proportion of gp10025-33 tetramer+ cells was found in the draining lymph nodes of mice that had received Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- cells (Figure 4K) compared to those who had received Pmel-1 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4K.

claim: Tumors from both Pmel-1 and Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- ACT groups had a similar density of infiltrating lymphocytes.
source: Tumors from both groups had a similar density of infiltrating lymphocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Knocking-out SLAMF6 in peptide-pulsed APCs enhances the response of Pmel-1 T cells.
source: Figure 5A shows that knocking-out SLAMF6 in peptide-pulsed APCs enhances the response of Pmel-1 T cells, attesting to the inhibitory effect of the trans positioning of SLAMF6.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA data in Figure 5A.

claim: A modest increase in function was observed in the SLAMF6 -/- T cells compared to the WT T cells when cultured with WT APCs.
source: A modest increase in function was observed in the SLAMF6 -/- T cells compared to the WT T cells when cultured with WT APCs, attesting to the improvement in the absence of cis positioned SLAMF6.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA data in Figure 5A.

claim: When SLAMF6-/- T cells were activated by SLAMF6-/- APCs, their cytokine secretion increased even more (p=0.001, Anova test).
source: However, when SLAMF6-/- T cells were activated by SLAMF6-/- APCs, their cytokine secretion increased even more (p=0.001, Anova test).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA data in Figure 5A.

claim: SLAMF6-deficient APCs are inherently better at activating T cells.
source: This finding suggests that not only the absence of SLAMF6 on the T cells improves their secretion capacity, but also SLAMF6-deficient APCs are inherently better.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the co-culture experiments.

claim: EL4 cells expressing SLAMF6 inhibited WT Pmel-1 T cells.
source: This observation was confirmed with the EL4 APCs (Figure 5C), which inhibited the WT Pmel-1 T cells, as expected, but surprisingly also inhibited the Pmel-1 x SLAMF6-/- CD8+ T cells, which were expected to be resistant to this effect.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA data in Figure 5C.

claim: EL4 cells expressing SLAMF6 also inhibited Pmel-1 x SLAMF6-/- CD8+ T cells.
source: This observation was confirmed with the EL4 APCs (Figure 5C), which inhibited the WT Pmel-1 T cells, as expected, but surprisingly also inhibited the Pmel-1 x SLAMF6-/- CD8+ T cells, which were expected to be resistant to this effect.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA data in Figure 5C.

claim: The inhibitory effect of SLAMF6 derives from both in cis and in trans interactions.
source: These results show that the inhibitory effect of SLAMF6 derives from both in cis and in trans interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the co-culture experiments.

claim: SAP transcript was found at similar levels in WT and SLAMF6 -/- lymphocytes.
source: However, while SAP transcript was found at similar levels in WT and SLAMF6 -/- lymphocytes, SAP protein was not detectable in SLAMF6 -/- cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-PCR data in Figure 6A.

claim: SAP protein was not detectable in SLAMF6 -/- cells.
source: However, while SAP transcript was found at similar levels in WT and SLAMF6 -/- lymphocytes, SAP protein was not detectable in SLAMF6 -/- cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6B.

claim: The discrepancy between SAP transcript and protein could be due to the rapid degradation of cytoplasmic SAP in its unbound form.
source: The discrepancy between the transcript and the protein could be due to the rapid degradation of cytoplasmic SAP in its unbound form.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the results to explain the observed discrepancy.

claim: SAP protein deficiency implies that SLAMF6 is its major anchor in non-activated CD8+ T cells.
source: SAP protein deficiency also implies that SLAMF6 is its major anchor in non-activated CD8+ T cells, even though SAP also mediates the inhibitory activity of PD-1 (Peled et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: PD-1 expression is more than two-fold increased in 7 day activated Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- lymphocytes compared to Pmel-1.
source: As shown in Figure 3F, PD-1 expression is more than two-fold increased in 7 day activated Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- lymphocytes compared to Pmel-1, but, as we have shown, this gap did not affect functionality.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3F.

claim: PD-1 overexpression can represent the failure of this receptor to generate a negative feedback loop in over-activated T cells.
source: Thus, PD-1 overexpression can represent the failure of this receptor to generate a negative feedback loop in over-activated T cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the observed PD-1 expression pattern.

claim: No difference in phosphorylated rpS6 was found in the Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- T cells.
source: Next, we measured by flow cytometry the level of phosphorylated ribosomal protein S6 (rpS6), an integrator of important signaling pathways, including PI3K/AKT/mTOR and RAS-ERK (Figure 6C). No difference in phosphorylated rpS6 was found in the Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6C.

claim: T-bet increased more than twofold in activated Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- splenocytes.
source: The most prominent regulator found was T-bet, which increased more than twofold in activated Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- splenocytes, followed by Eomes (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 6D.

claim: T-bet was originally described as the key transcription factor defining type 1 T helper (Th) cells.
source: T-bet was originally described as the key transcription factor defining type 1 T helper (Th) cells; it has since been found to play a major role in the acquisition of effector functions by CD8+ T cells (Szabo et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Type one inflammatory signals induce T-bet expression.
source: Type one inflammatory signals induce T-bet expression (Joshi et al., 2007), which is in line with the intensive IFN-γ secretion we observed by the Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- lymphocytes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Five days after the end of a 7-day activation course, Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- T cells displayed similar levels of PD-1, CD244 (SLAMF4), and TIM-3 to those in the Pmel-1 T cells, but higher expression of LAG-3.
source: Five days after the end of a 7-day activation course, Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- T cells displayed similar levels of PD-1, CD244 (SLAMF4), and TIM-3 to those in the Pmel-1 T cells, but higher expression of LAG-3 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6E.

claim: Blocking LAG-3 on Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- lymphocytes increased their cytokine secretion significantly.
source: As expected, blocking LAG-3 on Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- lymphocytes increased their cytokine secretion significantly, whereas it did not affect Pmel-1 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA data in Figure 6F.

claim: Blocking LAG-3 did not affect Pmel-1 cells.
source: As expected, blocking LAG-3 on Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- lymphocytes increased their cytokine secretion significantly, whereas it did not affect Pmel-1 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA data in Figure 6F.

claim: Knocking out SLAMF6 together with LAG-3 blockade resulted in a three-fold increase in IFN-γ production.
source: Overall, knocking out SLAMF6 together with LAG-3 blockade resulted in a three-fold increase in IFN-γ production (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA data in Figure 6F.

claim: Mice treated by the combination of SLAMF6-deficient T cells and anti-LAG-3 antibody showed faster reduction and disappearance of their tumors.
source: Mice treated by the combination of SLAMF6-deficient T cells and anti-LAG-3 antibody showed faster reduction and disappearance of their tumors (Figure 6H), apparent already on day 16 (p=0.04) (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by in vivo tumor growth data in Figure 6H and I.

claim: Blocking the compensatory rise of LAG-3 on SLAMF6-/- T cells improved their anti-tumor effect.
source: These results demonstrate that blocking the compensatory rise of LAG-3 on SLAMF6-/- T cells improved their anti-tumor effect even further.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the combination therapy experiments.

claim: SLAMF6 is a receptor whose absence significantly improves CD8+-mediated tumor regression.
source: The data obtained identify SLAMF6 as a receptor whose absence significantly improves CD8+-mediated tumor regression, suggesting that it is an inhibitory checkpoint.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: X-linked lymphoproliferative disease (XLP) is a complex genetic immune dysfunction caused by a SAP mutation.
source: Historically, SFRs were studied for their part in X-linked lymphoproliferative disease (XLP), a complex genetic immune dysfunction caused by a SAP mutation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as background information.

claim: XLP is characterized by a compromised immune response to Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) but also by unrestrained T lymphoblast proliferation.
source: XLP is characterized by a compromised immune response to Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) but also by unrestrained T lymphoblast proliferation, which is not necessarily EBV-induced.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as background information about XLP.

claim: SLAMF6 was considered a receptor with a dual function, depending on the interplay between SAP and SHP-1 and SHP-2.
source: In this situation, SLAMF6 was considered a receptor with a dual function, depending on the interplay between SAP and SHP-1 and SHP-2, protein phosphatases that bind to tyrosines on the cytoplasmic tail of the receptor (Veillette, 2010; Cannons et al., 2011; Detre et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Veillette showed differing effects of SLAMF6 on NK cells, enhancing function in the priming phase while suppressing cells in the effector-phase.
source: SLAMF6 duality was echoed in data from Veillette that showed differing effects of SLAMF6 on NK cells, enhancing function in the priming phase while suppressing cells in the effector-phase (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Mice lacking individual SFRs exhibit minor immune deviations.
source: Also, mice lacking individual SFRs exhibit minor immune deviations (Wu and Veillette, 2016; Cannons et al., 2011; Veillette, 2010; Calpe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Targeting SLAMF6 with its soluble ectodomain yielded CD8+ T cells that do not need IL-2 supplementation to eradicate established melanoma.
source: In the past, we described that targeting SLAMF6 with its soluble ectodomain yielded CD8+ T cells that do not need IL-2 supplementation, either in vitro or in vivo, to eradicate established melanoma (Eisenberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: Knocking-out SLAMF6 in murine antigen-specific CD8+ T cells disclosed an unequivocal inhibitory role for the receptor.
source: A key finding using the new Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- mice described in this manuscript is the absence, in fact, of a dichotomy in SLAMF6 action in effector T cells. On the contrary, knocking-out SLAMF6 in murine antigen-specific CD8+ T cells disclosed an unequivocal inhibitory role for the receptor.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a key finding of the study.

claim: The absence of viable SAP in SLAMF6 -/- lymphocytes hints that this adaptor takes a major part in the inhibitory effect of SLAMF6.
source: The absence of viable SAP in SLAMF6 -/- lymphocytes hints that this adaptor takes a major part in the inhibitory effect of SLAMF6.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the SAP protein data.

claim: The synapse is a subcellular structure involved in the effect of SLAMF6 and is crucial for its study.
source: The synapse is a subcellular structure involved in the effect of SLAMF6 and is crucial for its study (Zhao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The improved IFNγ secretion of SLAMF6-/- T cells when co-cultured with SLAMF6-lacking APCs compared to WT APCs implies that an inherent mechanism in the antigen presenting cells is responsible for the effect.
source: However, the improved IFNγ secretion of SLAMF6-/- T cells, when co-cultured with SLAMF6-lacking APCs compared to WT APCs, implies that an inherent mechanism, most likely lack of cis-inhibition in the antigen presenting cells, is also responsible for the effect (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the co-culture experiments.

claim: The molecular mechanisms underlying the increased functional capacity of Pmel-1 T cells lacking SLAMF6 have common features with XLP.
source: The molecular mechanisms underlying the increased functional capacity of Pmel-1 T cells lacking SLAMF6 have common features with XLP, as the absence of SAP implies.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the mechanistic findings.

claim: While XLP is a global defect of all cell types of the immune system, the absence of SLAMF6 is remarkable for the enhanced functionality of CD8+ T cells.
source: But while XLP is a global defect of all cell types of the immune system, and therefore yields mixed derangements, the absence of SLAMF6 is remarkable for the enhanced functionality of CD8+ T cells, in which it is the dominating SFR.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a comparison between XLP and SLAMF6 deficiency.

claim: T-bet is a transcription factor that contributes to Th1 and Th17 phenotypes in CD4 T cells.
source: The transcriptional landscape of SLAMF6 -/- T cells was governed by the higher expression of T-bet. T-bet is a transcription factor that contributes to Th1 and Th17 phenotypes in CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as background information about T-bet.

claim: T-bet is prevalent in cytolytic innate lymphocytes residing in tissues and B cells of mouse strains prone to autoimmunity.
source: T-bet is prevalent in cytolytic innate lymphocytes residing in tissues and B cells of mouse strains prone to autoimmunity (Plank et al., 2017; Nixon and Li, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The increased activity of T-bet in SLAMF6 -/- CD8+ T cells implies that T-bet-regulated pathways may operate in CD8+ T cells in the absence of functioning SLAMF6.
source: The increased activity of T-bet in SLAMF6 -/- CD8+ T cells implies that T-bet-regulated pathways may operate in CD8+ T cells in the absence of functioning SLAMF6, generating 'type 1' inflammatory traits and high cytotoxicity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the T-bet findings.

claim: The improved production of IFN-γ and GM-CSF, in parallel with reduced IL-10 and IL-13, is typical for type one phenotypes.
source: The improved production of IFN-γ and GM-CSF, in parallel with reduced IL-10 and IL-13, is also typical for type one phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the cytokine profile.

claim: SLAMF6 should be distinguished from typical exhaustion markers because it is expressed on CD8+ T cells, regardless of their state of activation.
source: SLAMF6 should be distinguished from typical exhaustion markers because it is expressed on CD8+ T cells, regardless of their state of activation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a distinguishing feature of SLAMF6.

claim: Yigit et al. suggested that blocking SLAMF6 using an antibody can correct the exhaustion phase of T cells.
source: Yigit et al. suggested that blocking SLAMF6 using an antibody can correct the exhaustion phase of T cells (Yigit et al., 2019), but we favor the notion that SLAMF6 hampers T cells at any stage, as reflected from the functional superiority of short-term activated Pmel-1 T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to Yigit et al.'s work.

claim: SLAMF6 hampers T cells at any stage, as reflected from the functional superiority of short-term activated Pmel-1 T cells.
source: Yigit et al. suggested that blocking SLAMF6 using an antibody can correct the exhaustion phase of T cells (Yigit et al., 2019), but we favor the notion that SLAMF6 hampers T cells at any stage, as reflected from the functional superiority of short-term activated Pmel-1 T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: Depleting SLAMF6 improved CD8+ T cells in the short and long-term.
source: Depleting SLAMF6 improved CD8+ T cells in the short and long-term, as was most evident when the WT Pmel-1 cells induced the regression of melanoma only for a limited period while the Pmel-1 x SLAMF6 -/- cells led to lasting responses in mice (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by in vivo data in Figure 4H.

claim: SLAMF6 is an important checkpoint receptor with a significant inhibitory effect on T cells.
source: From the results presented here, we conclude that SLAMF6 is an important checkpoint receptor with a significant inhibitory effect on T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The balance between SLAMF6 and LAG-3, and the enhancing effect of LAG3 blocking suggests that targeting both may have a valuable combinatorial, and perhaps even a synergistic, effect.
source: The balance between SLAMF6 and LAG-3, and the enhancing effect of LAG3 blocking suggests that targeting both may have a valuable combinatorial, and perhaps even a synergistic, effect (Figure 6G–I).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by combination therapy data in Figure 6G-I.

claim: In the absence of SLAMF6, CD8+ T cells acquire stronger reactivity against tumor cells.
source: In summary, we have shown that SLAMF6 is a constitutive inhibitory immune receptor; in its absence, CD8+ T cells acquire stronger reactivity against tumor cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary conclusion.

claim: The strong effector trait is attributed to a series of T-bet-mediated transcriptional events that drive CD8+ T cells to exert strong cytotoxicity and achieve long-lasting tumor control.
source: The strong effector trait is attributed to a series of T-bet-mediated transcriptional events that drive CD8+ T cells to exert strong cytotoxicity and achieve long-lasting tumor control.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a mechanistic conclusion.

claim: SLAMF6 is an attractive target for the development of checkpoint inhibitors for systemic treatment of cancer and for the improvement of antitumor cellular therapies.
source: SLAMF6 is an attractive target for the development of checkpoint inhibitors for systemic treatment of cancer and for the improvement of antitumor cellular therapies.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a translational implication of the findings.

claim: SLAMF6 transcript rises at 6 hr of activation in CD4+ T cells.
source: The SLAMF6 transcript appears in cluster C, rising at 6 hr of activation and staying high after that (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA sequencing data in Figure 1G.

claim: CD44 encodes a glycoprotein that takes part in T cell activation.
source: Other genes in cluster C are CD44, encoding a glycoprotein that takes part in T cell activation (Huet et al., 1989), and CD28 and ICOS, which encode co-stimulatory immune receptors (Turka et al., 1990; Dong et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: CD28 and ICOS encode co-stimulatory immune receptors.
source: Other genes in cluster C are CD44, encoding a glycoprotein that takes part in T cell activation (Huet et al., 1989), and CD28 and ICOS, which encode co-stimulatory immune receptors (Turka et al., 1990; Dong et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.

claim: The increase in the transcription of receptors that are stably expressed at all times may hint at enhanced recruitment and degradation of these receptors during activation, possibly in the immune synapse.
source: The increase in the transcription of receptors that are stably expressed at all times may hint at enhanced recruitment and degradation of these receptors during activation, possibly in the immune synapse (Onnis and Baldari, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results as a speculation with a supporting citation.

claim: On day 23, the mean tumor volume was 431 mm3 in the SLAMF6-expressing melanomas, compared to 137 mm3 in the non-modified tumors (p=0.04, Student's t-test).
source: The B16-F10/mhgp100/SLAMF6+ tumors grew more aggressively: on day 23, the mean tumor volume was 431 mm3 in the SLAMF6-expressing melanomas, compared to 137 mm3 in the non-modified tumors (p=0.04, Student's t-test) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and supported by tumor growth data in Figure 2E.

claim: Pmel-1 mice carry a rearranged TCR specific for a 9-mer epitope (25-32) from murine Pmel 17.
source: The Pmel-1 mice carry a rearranged TCR specific for a 9-mer epitope (25-32) from murine Pmel 17, overexpressed on transformed melanocytes and homologous to the human melanoma-associated antigen gp100.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the mouse model.

claim: Pmel-1 TCR is specific for an epitope overexpressed on transformed melanocytes and homologous to the human melanoma-associated antigen gp100.
source: The Pmel-1 mice carry a rearranged TCR specific for a 9-mer epitope (25-32) from murine Pmel 17, overexpressed on transformed melanocytes and homologous to the human melanoma-associated antigen gp100.
